sec.p: Pesticides pose a serious public health problem, with well-documented links to a range of adverse health outcomes including acute poisonings as well as cancers, neurological disorders, and reproductive harms. Pesticide self-poisoning remains one of the most common methods of suicide worldwide. The widespread use of pesticides within agri-food systems is also damaging the environment and ecosystems. Despite growing scientific evidence, effective policy responses including within the EU are lacking and existing regulation is being weakened, often in the context of intense industry lobbying and opposition. This workshop addresses a critical gap in public health discourse by examining these industries as major commercial determinants of health (CDOH) and inequity. The workshop has three main objectives: first, to strengthen understanding of the harms driven by the pesticide industry and the unequal global burden of these harms; second, to examine how pesticide industry actors shape science, policy, and public norms and understanding to protect their commercial interests; and third, to identify ways to counter these harms. Presentations of key examples will highlight industry strategies such as manufacturing doubt and weakening or delaying policy action. The Pecha Kucha style presentations will provide illuminating examples of research examining the pesticide industry as a powerful commercial determinant of health and its activities surrounding EU and international chemical and environmental policy. Analyses of the pesticide industry’s framing of pesticide safety, role in food security, and regulation, and its engagement with pesticide suicide prevention will be presented. A framework for examining how industries like the pesticide and other petrochemical industries produce and benefit from inequities will be introduced. Ongoing work within WHO on understanding the pesticide and other elements of the agrochemical industry as a commercial determinant of health will be shared also. The workshop brings together evidence on how the pesticide and other petrochemical industries function as major drivers of healthy and equity, and links EU policy dynamics with broader implications for global health governance and equity. By drawing parallels with lessons from tobacco control and other areas, the workshop will provide actionable insights into how harmful industry influence can be effectively countered. Participants will engage in a facilitated discussion to identify opportunities for collaboration, research priorities, and advocacy strategies to counter pesticide, and other petrochemical, industry influence. Overall, the workshop seeks to move beyond problem identification towards collective action, equipping participants with the knowledge and tools to address pesticide harms as part of the broader CDOH agenda.

sec.title: Key messages
sec.p: • The pesticide industry is a powerful but under-recognised commercial determinant of health that shapes science and policy to delay effective regulation.
• Strengthening collaboration and applying lessons from tobacco control are essential to counter industry influence and advance health-promoting pesticide policies.
